title: Trigonometry B: Elevation, Depression, Bearings

findings.finding: The worked examples depend on substantial right-triangle trigonometry prerequisites without an opening review.
findings.breakdown: Following the three examples requires identifying side roles, selecting a ratio, using inverse sine and solving side equations with the unknown in either the numerator or denominator.
findings.checked: All preceding teaching concerns angle interpretation and angle relationships. The immediately preceding topic and its supplied practice do not rehearse these trigonometric methods.
findings.assumptions: Right-angled trigonometry was taught previously in the separate course booklet. Students have scientific calculators in degree mode.

repair.proposal: Before p6-example-activity, add four short items within one page: (1) In triangle ABC, B=90°. Relative to A, identify AB, BC and AC, then complete sin A, cos A and tan A. [Adjacent, opposite, hypotenuse; BC/AC, AB/AC, BC/AB.] (2) Opposite side=8 cm and hypotenuse=13 cm. Write an equation and find θ to the nearest degree. [sin θ=8/13; 38°.] (3) Solve tan(42°)=x/18 to 1 d.p. [16.2.] (4) Solve tan(35°)=12/x to 1 d.p. [17.1.]

findings.doneWhen: The review rehearses the prerequisite decisions and equation forms used directly by the examples.

findings.finding: Vary the depression angle while holding the cliff height fixed.
findings.breakdown: The run exposes how increasing depression angle reduces horizontal distance.
findings.checked: Using d = 36/tan θ gives 99 m, 62 m and 43 m. The unpatterned question gives 107 m. All methods appear in p6.
findings.assumptions: A scientific calculator in degree mode is available.

repair.proposal: Append parts under p8-q2's nearest-metre instruction. Add only this instruction: 'Predict whether each distance will increase or decrease before calculating.' (b) Same 36 m cliff, depression angle 20°. Answer: 99 m. (c) Same cliff, 30°. Answer: 62 m. (d) Same cliff, 40°. Answer: 43 m. (e) A boat is viewed from a 50 m cliff at a depression angle of 25°. Find its horizontal distance from the base. Answer: 107 m. Height stays fixed through b–d while angle varies.

findings.doneWhen: The three fixed-height variations and one unpatterned follow-up are appended.

findings.finding: Hold the acute compass angle fixed while changing its quadrant.
findings.breakdown: The sequence exposes how the quadrant determines the conversion to a true bearing.
findings.checked: The existing six parts vary both angle and quadrant. All proposed conversions are correct and use methods available by the end of this topic.
findings.assumptions: Each added diagram supplies its marked acute angle under the existing question instruction.

repair.proposal: Append one instruction line: 'Predict how the true bearing will change before completing each part.' Add diagrams for (g) 20° east of North [N20°E, 020°], (h) 20° east of South [S20°E, 160°], (i) 20° west of South [S20°W, 200°], and (j) 20° west of North [N20°W, 340°]. Follow with unpatterned part (k), 37° west of North [N37°W, 323°]. The acute angle stays fixed through g–j; the quadrant varies.

findings.doneWhen: The added parts isolate the effect of quadrant before an unpatterned conversion.

findings.finding: The reverse-bearing example uses cointerior angles without an opening rehearsal of that relationship.
findings.breakdown: Obtaining 116° from 64° requires recalling that cointerior angles between parallel lines sum to 180°. The worked caption names the relationship but does not rehearse it.
findings.checked: Earlier p4 teaching covers alternate angles, triangle sums and right angles, but not cointerior angles. The immediately preceding compass-bearing topic rehearses full-turn subtraction, so that piece has been removed from the finding.
findings.assumptions: Cointerior angles are previously taught angle knowledge. No calculator is needed.

repair.proposal: Before p20-information-text, add three short diagrams of parallel vertical lines crossed by a transversal. In each, mark one interior angle and ask for its cointerior partner: (a) 64° [116°], (b) 105° [75°], (c) 132° [48°]. Keep the review within one page.

findings.doneWhen: Students rehearse finding a cointerior angle before the reverse-bearing example.

findings.finding: Six of the claimed pairs repeat complete tasks with unchanged prompts, givens and mathematical diagrams, without an explicit instructional purpose.
findings.breakdown: The later copies repeat an identical decision and calculation rather than providing fresh numerical practice.
findings.checked: Confirmed c/e, d/j and f/k across p22–p23; p24-q3-b/h; p23-q2-a with p24-q3-i; and p21-part-2 with p26-q7a. The claimed p22-q1-h/p24-q3-d pair is excluded because its givens differ: 80° versus 70°. No retrieval or comparison purpose is stated for the six confirmed pairs.
findings.assumptions: Question diagrams are compared using their supplied specifications, excluding solution annotations.

repair.proposal: Retain each earlier copy and change the later copy's given angle, preserving its structure: p23-q2-e, clockwise 115° at A [B from A=115°]; p23-q2-j, anticlockwise 245° at A [B from A=115°]; p23-q2-k, anticlockwise 120° at B [A from B=240°]; p24-q3-h, clockwise 130° at B [B from A=310°]; p24-q3-i, anticlockwise 290° at A [A from B=250°]; p26-q7a, clockwise 125° at A [A from B=305°]. Update each diagram to match its revised given.

findings.doneWhen: Each of the six later copies retains its method and structure with different numerical givens and the stated answer.

findings.finding: Rotate both equal-length journey directions by the same numerical amount.
findings.breakdown: The follow-up connects a common change in leg bearings with the change in the direct bearing.
findings.checked: Equal legs on bearings 050° and 080° produce direct bearing 065°, using the isosceles-triangle reasoning already required in p30-q18. This is 20° clockwise from part b's 045°.
findings.assumptions: The equal-leg condition PC = CQ is retained.

repair.proposal: Append optional parts: (e) 'In part b, keep PC = CQ but change the bearing of C from P to 050° and the bearing of Q from C to 080°. Find the bearing of Q from P.' Answer: 065°. (f) 'How much has the bearing of Q from P changed from part b?' Answer: 20° clockwise.

findings.doneWhen: The two numerical follow-up parts and their answers are appended.

findings.finding: The introductory example introduces 30° from the given 060° bearing without writing the connecting calculation.
findings.breakdown: The example hides the decision that converts a bearing measured from north into the triangle angle used with cosine.
findings.checked: The triangle diagram supplies the derived 30° label, but no displayed line explains its origin. Earlier complementary-angle work establishes the skill without supplying this example's missing connection.
findings.assumptions: Students know complementary angles and are learning to choose reference angles for bearing calculations.

repair.proposal: In Step 2, before the cosine equation, add: 'The angle between AB and east is 90°−60°=30°.'

findings.doneWhen: The example explicitly connects the supplied bearing to the angle used in its trigonometric equation.

findings.finding: The topic returns to trigonometric side calculations without reviewing the prerequisite decisions used by its worked example.
findings.breakdown: The equation cos(30°)=x/3 requires identifying adjacent and hypotenuse, selecting cosine and solving for a numerator unknown.
findings.checked: The immediately preceding bearing-scenarios topic constructs component triangles but does not calculate their sides using trigonometry. The trigonometric calculations on p6 belong to an older topic.
findings.assumptions: Right-angled trigonometry was taught previously. Scientific calculators are available in degree mode.

repair.proposal: Before p33-method-block, add three short items within one page: (a) On a supplied right triangle with a marked 35° angle, label opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse. (b) A right triangle has hypotenuse 12 km and unknown side x adjacent to 35°. Write an equation for x. [cos(35°)=x/12.] (c) Solve x/18=sin(40°), giving x to 1 decimal place. [x=18 sin(40°)=11.6.]

findings.doneWhen: The opening review rehearses side classification, ratio choice and the equation manipulation used directly in the example.

findings.finding: In the supplied practice order, the rally and NE/NW plane problems precede the questions that bridge their combined demands.
findings.breakdown: After supplied single-journey triangles, the rally removes the diagram and combines speed–time calculations with a return leg. The plane then requires constructing a rotated two-leg right triangle and calculating a bearing from it.
findings.checked: Read the supplied practice order: both questions occur immediately after p34-q1. Later p36-q7 and p38-q14 develop return-leg interpretation; p39-q15–q17 develop non-cardinal right triangles and calculated bearings. Those existing questions provide the bridges.
findings.assumptions: The supplied practice array is the classroom order, as stated by the candidate. Speed–distance–time, Pythagoras and inverse trigonometry are prior learning.

repair.proposal: Move the whole p41-q22 task immediately after p38-q14. Move the whole p40-q20 task immediately after p39-q17. Preserve their stems and all parts.

findings.doneWhen: The existing return-leg and non-cardinal-triangle preparation precedes the respective combined problems.

findings.finding: Compare the ships' separation and relative bearing after half the elapsed time.
findings.breakdown: The follow-up exposes proportional distance scaling while preserving the triangle's angles.
findings.checked: After four hours the perpendicular journey lengths are 80 and 140 nautical miles, giving separation sqrt(80² + 140²) = 161.25 nautical miles. The relative bearing remains 276°45′. Only methods required by the existing question are needed.
findings.assumptions: Both ships maintain their stated constant speeds and bearings.

repair.proposal: Append optional parts: (c) 'How far apart are the ships after 4 hours? Give your answer in nautical miles to 2 decimal places.' Answer: 161.25 nautical miles. (d) 'What is the bearing of the second ship from the first after 4 hours, to the nearest minute? Explain why it is the same as your answer to part b.' Answer: 276°45′; both journey distances halve, preserving the triangle's angles.

findings.doneWhen: The two numerical follow-up parts and their expected answers are appended.

findings.finding: Connect the vertical-reference angle with the angle of depression in the existing diagram.
findings.breakdown: The follow-up compares the two reference angles at B as the line of sight changes.
findings.checked: p4 teaches complementary angles and equal elevation and depression angles. The proposed answers are correct and require only those methods.
findings.assumptions: The horizontal and vertical references remain perpendicular when the elevation changes.

repair.proposal: Append optional parts to p5-q3: (c) Find θ. [68°] (d) If the angle of elevation at A increases to 32°, what is the new angle of depression from B to A? [32°] (e) What is the new value of θ? [58°]

findings.doneWhen: The optional parts connect equal elevation and depression angles with their complementary vertical-reference angle.

findings.finding: Explore how the flagpole height changes when the horizontal distance doubles and both elevation angles remain fixed.
findings.breakdown: The follow-up exposes proportional scaling in the difference between two tangent calculations.
findings.checked: The original calculation is 200(tan 36°−tan 34°). Replacing 200 by 400 gives approximately 20.8 m and exactly doubles the unrounded result.
findings.assumptions: Scientific calculators are available in degree mode.

repair.proposal: Append optional parts: (b) At another building, the elevation angles to the bottom and top of a flagpole are again 34° and 36°, but the horizontal distance is 400 m. Calculate the flagpole height to 1 decimal place. [20.8 m.] (c) Using unrounded calculations, how many times the original flagpole height is this? [2 times.] (d) Explain why doubling the horizontal distance doubles the calculated flagpole height when both angles remain fixed. [Both calculated heights double, so their difference doubles.]

findings.doneWhen: The numerical follow-up connects the two-height calculation with proportional scaling.

findings.finding: Compare eastward distances at fixed journey length as bearings change through complementary and supplementary pairs.
findings.breakdown: The sequence exposes equal eastward distances for routes reflected across east.
findings.checked: For a 4 km journey, the eastward distances at 055°, 035°, 125°, 145° and 072° are respectively 3.28, 2.29, 3.28, 2.29 and 3.80 km. All routes lie east of the starting point and can be solved with the taught acute-angle methods.
findings.assumptions: Scientific calculators are available in degree mode.

repair.proposal: Make the existing 055° task part (a), with the common instruction to find the eastward distance to 2 decimal places. Add one line: 'Predict which eastward distances will be equal before calculating.' Add (b) Walk 4 km on bearing 035° [2.29 km], (c) 125° [3.28 km], (d) 145° [2.29 km], and unpatterned part (e) 072° [3.80 km]. Journey length and requested component stay fixed; bearing varies.

findings.doneWhen: The run compares the paired bearings and finishes with an unpatterned calculation.

protectedGroups.observation: The same descending line of sight gives depression only when the marked angle starts at the horizontal.
protectedGroups.varies: The reference side of the marked angle: horizontal or vertical.
protectedGroups.invariant: Triangle orientation and upper-left observation vertex.

protectedGroups.observation: One line of sight supports depression at the upper observer, elevation at the lower observer, and neither when measured from the vertical.
protectedGroups.varies: The location and reference side of the marked angle.
protectedGroups.invariant: A rising diagonal with a vertical right side and horizontal references.

protectedGroups.observation: An angle measured clockwise from north is used directly, with a leading zero.
protectedGroups.invariant: North reference, northeast quadrant and three-digit notation.

protectedGroups.observation: Angles on opposite sides of east require subtraction from or addition to 90°.
protectedGroups.varies: Which side of east contains OA, and the given angle.

protectedGroups.observation: Bearings approach south and continue beyond it, changing from subtraction to addition around 180°.
protectedGroups.varies: OA's position relative to south and the given angle; the cardinal case uses a west reference.

protectedGroups.observation: The same direction can be specified using complementary angles from south and west.
protectedGroups.varies: Reference direction and given angle: 47° from south or 43° from west.
protectedGroups.invariant: OA's direction and true bearing; these are different givens, not duplicate tasks.

protectedGroups.observation: Bearings approach west and continue beyond it, changing from subtraction to addition around 270°.
protectedGroups.varies: Given angle and side of west containing OA.
protectedGroups.invariant: West reference and clockwise bearing convention.

protectedGroups.observation: The triangle's vertical side can differ from the total object height: subtract known heights before solving, or add eye height afterwards.
protectedGroups.varies: Whether a vertical offset is removed before the trig calculation or restored afterwards.
protectedGroups.invariant: A horizontal line through the observation point determines the triangle's vertical rise.

protectedGroups.observation: Two right-triangle calculations can isolate a gap by subtraction.
protectedGroups.varies: Common horizontal distance with two elevations versus common vertical height with two depressions.
protectedGroups.invariant: Calculate both distances from the same reference before subtracting.

protectedGroups.observation: The same direction can be represented by a compass bearing or a true bearing.
protectedGroups.invariant: Origin and northwest ray: N60°W and 300°T.

protectedGroups.observation: The same travel direction is expressed first as a true bearing and later as a compass bearing.
protectedGroups.invariant: Southwest direction and the 30° angle from South.

protectedGroups.observation: Horizontal and vertical component labels retain their meanings across all four travel quadrants.
protectedGroups.varies: Quadrant, angle, distance and bearing notation.
protectedGroups.invariant: The travel leg is the hypotenuse; x labels horizontal distance and y labels vertical distance.

protectedGroups.observation: The same requested bearing can be supplied directly or obtained from the other sector of a full turn.
protectedGroups.varies: The labelled sector is clockwise 105 degrees or complementary anticlockwise 255 degrees.
protectedGroups.invariant: Point arrangement, requested direction and resulting bearing.

protectedGroups.observation: A reflex clockwise bearing and its smaller anticlockwise complement describe the same direction.
protectedGroups.varies: The given angle is 280 degrees clockwise or 80 degrees anticlockwise.
protectedGroups.invariant: Point arrangement and requested bearing of A from B.

protectedGroups.observation: Changing the requested starting location changes the bearing even when the geometry and given angle stay fixed.
protectedGroups.varies: B from A versus A from B.
protectedGroups.invariant: The two locations, north references and 105-degree given at A.

protectedGroups.observation: A labelled angle is not automatically the requested bearing; its vertex and reference direction determine the calculation.
protectedGroups.varies: The starting vertex, direction of the segment and reference ray for the labelled angle.
protectedGroups.invariant: The value 54 degrees and the instruction to find B from A.

protectedGroups.observation: Turning both equal route legs through the same angle turns the direct direction through that angle.
protectedGroups.varies: Both given bearings increase by 90 degrees.
protectedGroups.invariant: Equal connected legs and the 30-degree difference between their bearings.

protectedGroups.observation: The set requires selecting opposite or adjacent components across directions, then removes the supplied reference-angle labels.
protectedGroups.varies: Quadrant, bearing notation, requested component and degree of annotation.
protectedGroups.invariant: A single journey is the hypotenuse of a right triangle and a cardinal displacement is required.

protectedGroups.observation: The paired tasks distinguish finding a component from finding the reverse bearing in two different quadrants.
protectedGroups.varies: Southeast versus southwest journey and the direction of the requested horizontal component.
protectedGroups.invariant: Each journey is followed by a component question and a reverse-bearing question.
